region: Northern Hemisphere; main lumber species from North America and Europe
description: Oak is one of the most widely used furniture and flooring hardwoods, sold mainly as red oak (e.g. Quercus rubra) and white oak (e.g. Quercus alba, and European Quercus robur). It is strong, open-pored, and common in cabinetry, flooring, barrels, and joinery, so many woodworkers generate a lot of oak dust.

hazards.summary: IARC classifies all wood dust as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancer of the nasal cavity and sinuses after long-term heavy exposure. This applies to every species, so dust control matters whatever you cut.
ACGIH names oak dust specifically as a confirmed human carcinogen (A1), one of only two woods with that class. The classification covers oak as a group rather than red or white oak separately.

Three workers in Quebec developed asthma from oak dust, confirmed by specific inhalation challenge in the lab. The species of oak is not given in the abstract; the UK HSE also lists asthma for oak in general.
The UK HSE lists sneezing for oak. A French study of beech and oak furniture workers found more sore throat and more twitchy airways as dust levels rose; it did not separate oak from beech.
The UK HSE lists eye irritation as a reported effect of oak dust. We did not find a primary paper describing this for oak specifically.

exposure_limits.note: 8-hour time-weighted average, as restated by OSHA

related_species_note: ACGIH also lists beech as A1. Hardwood-dust studies often pool oak and beech, so oak-only numbers are scarce.

notes_internal: Genus entry covering red and white oak; no evidence found that separates their hazards. Malo-1995 abstract does not name the oak species (Schlunssen-2018 table lists Quercus robur for oak rows). Bohadana-2000 pools beech and oak; used only as supporting evidence. Not used: 'silky oak' (Grevillea robusta, not Quercus) dermatitis reports; Frullania (liverwort on bark) dermatitis, which is from bark epiphytes, not oak wood, and not oak-specific; Spiewak 1994 and Aldunate 1998 (oak asthma, from Schlunssen table) not indexed in PubMed and not verified. Image prompt uses red oak as the representative. Absence of reports for a hazard is not evidence that this wood is safe.
